https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl.text: Image source, Europol Image caption, Europol shared video from the operation, including of police dogs searching cars By Olivia Ireland Published 2 hours ago One of the largest criminal networks smuggling drugs and people in the western Mediterranean has been dismantled, authorities have said. Europol said 78 people were arrested in Spain and Algeria in a bust of the network, that is also linked to other criminal activities including "violent robberies, extortion, illegal detentions, and money laundering". The group moved synthetic drugs from Spain and Portugal to Algeria, then used the return journey to smuggle migrants and weapons to the Spanish mainland and island of Ibiza on "ghost speedboats". Some of the items seized included 18 high-speed vessels valued at â¬5m (Â£4.2m), guns, more than â¬25,000 (Â£21,400) in cash and 15,000 MDMA pills. The sting, led by Spanish police, involved searches in 17 locations in Spain, including Alicante, AlmerÃ­a, Cartagena and Murcia. Europol said the group had "evolved from drug trafficking into a duel-flow criminal enterprise designed to maximise profits" with outbound routes from Spain and Portugal to Algeria. "The smuggling focused on synthetic drugs (such as MDMA), firearms, and explosives. Along routine routes from Algeria to Spain, the group smuggled migrants, charging up to â¬12,000 (Â£10,200) per person," Europol's statement said. "In just one trip, over 50 migrants could be smuggled. All in all, profits from migrant smuggling alone are estimated to be more than â¬24m (Â£20m)." The network also provided services to other organised crime groups, "facilitating the movement of illicit goods and people across the Western Mediterranean". "Investigators believe the network coordinated multiple trafficking flows. Synthetic drugs, and sometimes people, were moved from France and Spain to Algeria, while cannabis resin, weapons, and migrants were transported from Algeria to Spain." Often, the group used a fleet of high-powered speedboats to conduct rapid maritime operations. This included "ghost speedboats" which are designed to avoid registration and detection, which are prohibited in Spain. "The group used these boats to organise transfers in international waters near the Spanish coastline," Europol said. "Once the cargo or migrants were handed over at sea, other network members arranged onward transport by land. "Migrants were often carried in overcrowded boats without lighting or life jackets, frequently under extreme weather conditions. "Investigators believe suspects perpetrated sexual assaults, physical abuse, and placed migrants in inhuman conditions in makeshift housing." The suspects were primarily of Algerian origin and had connections to criminal groups in France, Belgium, Portugal, Italy and Poland. Other objects seized in the police sting included satellite phones, GPS devices, encrypted communication tools and satellite dishes. The announcement comes a week after roughly 78,000 migrants fled into the Spanish North African territory of Ceuta that was blamed on online rumours about an open border. Most of the migrants returned to Morocco but between 3,000 and 5,000 remain in the territory, the exclave's leader Juan JesÃºs Vivas said. https://www.politico.eu/article/green-pa.text: LONDON — Keir Starmer’s old seat in the Commons is up for grabs. Zack Polanski is throwing everything at turning the Labour stronghold of Holborn and St. Pancras green. The leader of the left-wing populist Green Party is almost certain to be selected to stand in the Oct. 8 contest Thursday night, and activists have already flooded constituents with leaflets — with Polanski claiming they delivered 80,000 in just two hours Sunday. Labour is mounting its defense. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband — a popular figure on the Labour left who fronted a new set of trade sanctions on Israel this week — has already visited the seat, delivering a message of hope to Labour canvassers days after the former British prime minister announced he was standing down. Advertisement Advertisement Holborn and St. Pancras has had a Labour MP since its creation in 1983. The Greens would need to overturn Starmer’s 11,572 vote majority. For the two main parties in contention in the race to replace Starmer, there is a lot at stake. What’s at stake for Labour? This is Andy Burnham’s first test in a parliamentary by-election since becoming prime minister over the summer. For Labour, holding onto Holborn and St. Pancras would send a message that Labour’s image has been successfully divorced from Starmer’s unpopularity. It would also be an encouraging sign voters have accepted him as the new prime minister and are prepared to buy into his plan for government. The selection on Wednesday night of Camden Council Leader Sagal Abdi-Wali as the Labour candidate — who came to the U.K. as a refugee from Somalia — could also help the party’s chances. Reform UK spokesperson Zia Yusuf attacked Abdi-Wali’s background when she emerged as the frontrunner, and Labour will likely make the argument for progressive voters to back Abdi-Wali in a show of strength against Nigel Farage’s party. However, losing a seat that has been deemed safe for so long would be damaging for both Burnham and the party, as it would suggest that the reputational damage Labour suffered under Starmer had stuck. Advertisement Advertisement Sending such a high-profile party figure as the foreign secretary to address campaigners, while canvassers have already hit the streets, is a telling sign in a seat that historically should be a slam dunk for anyone wearing a red rosette. What’s at stake for Greens? A win for the Greens could be significant for two reasons. First, if Polanski wins the nomination to be the party’s candidate, it would put party leader in the House of Commons. It would allow them to argue the party still has momentum and has not peaked. The Gorton and Denton victory in February was the first time the Greens had got an MP into parliament via a by-election. But since Burnham took office, Polanski has had more difficulty cutting through, while a so-called “Burnham bounce” has hit the Greens’ poll ratings. Green candidate Geraldine Coggins came a disappointing third in the Manchester mayoral election in July, despite a significant ground and social media campaign by the party. However, a win in London could revitalize the party and show Burnham that he is still at risk of hemorrhaging left-wing support to the Greens unless he listens to certain demands — such as the public ownership of water, a wealth tax, and rent controls. The fight Holborn and St. Pancras has never previously been fought as a two-horse race between Labour and the Greens. Advertisement Advertisement Keir Starmer is pictured on the sidelines of the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Isabel Infantes via Getty Images Back in 2024, the Greens did not make a big play for the seat. During that race, it was independent candidate Andrew Feinstein — who later went on to be involved with Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana’s Your Party project — who posed the biggest threat to Starmer. Feinstein ran on a pro-Gaza, anti-austerity ticket, and managed to make a dent in the then-PM’s majority, winning 18.9% of the vote. Feinstein will not run this time, which could mean that his support transfers to the Greens, rather than Labour. Even then, combined Green and Feinstein support totaled 29%, compared to Starmer’s 49%, at the last general election. Moreover, this time they will not be able to present themselves as a protest vote against Starmer personally. It would help the Greens if university students are back before the vote as there are dozens of private and university-run accommodation buildings in the areas. But the short election timetable means most will not have moved in before September 22 — the deadline to register to vote. There’s also a large Muslim community in the seat — around 20% — which both parties will want to attract. Advertisement Advertisement In 2024, the war in Gaza was a major issue that pushed voters away from Labour. Burnham has said that the party’s position under Starmer was wrong, and is taking a stronger stance against the Israeli government. Restrictions on buying goods made in Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank were announced Tuesday. The battle lines The by-election might become a battle of competing national visions. Green supporters argue that Burnham will be prime minister regardless of the outcome, and that having Polanski as an MP will add to pressure on the government in parliament from the left. Meanwhile, Labour is selling Burnham’s vision for the future. “We can go out in this by-election and really talk with pride about what Andy’s new government in doing,” Miliband told campaigners last weekend. “He has a big argument about how the country needs to change; now it’s up to us in Holborn and St. Pancras to win back the progressive voters.” Abdi-Wali told the Camden New Journal in August that she thought Starmer should not step down as MP and described him as “really inspirational.” The constituency faces a number of specific local challenges. Despite this area of north London often being associated with liberal elite circles, the area is grappling with a housing crisis, high levels of deprivation, and more than a decade of chaos from the stalled HS2 project. Candidates will have to explain on the doorstep how they would change any of this if elected. Those details may emerge in coming weeks, and crucially during a hustings. But for now, it seems the first stage of battle will be over who can sell the most convincing message of hope. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dw.com/en/airport-malaria-in.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MsNM Malaria is only transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes Image: James Gathany/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Eight people are known to have contracted malaria in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport in central Germany since July; three of them have died . Those affected are mostly employees of the airport operator Fraport. The Frankfurt Public Health Department believes the outbreak is due to "airport malaria," which occurs when a female Anopheles mosquito carrying the malaria parasite travels by aircraft to a country where the disease is not common from one where it is , bites a person and infects their red blood cells. "We are dealing with a very rare occurrence, not a new frequent disease in Germany," said Achim Hörauf, the director of the Institute for Medical Microbiology, Immunology and Parasitology at Bonn's University Hospital (UKB), in a press release. Several die from rare 'airport malaria' in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Airport malaria is very infrequent The last documented case of airport malaria in Germany before the current ones was in 2023, according to the Epidemiologisches Bulletin of the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an online journal that regularly provides information on infectious diseases and public health. Normally, those with the disease in Germany were infected elsewhere and brought it back during a long-haul trip. But a mosquito can make its way to Germany as a "stowaway" if it was trapped in a suitcase or in clothing. Hörauf said that under certain circumstances, it might be able to survive in warmer areas of an airport. Frankfurt cases are of dangerous malaria tropica According to a UKB press release, the cases in Frankfurt involve malaria tropica , which is considered to be the most dangerous and potentially life-threatening form of malaria. To contract the disease, a person needs to be bitten by a female anopheles mosquito infected with the Plasmodium falciparum parasite. This pathogen passes to the human and then attacks the red blood vessels. "Simply put, it can lead to many small blockages in the blood vessels," explained Hörauf. "Depending on which organ is affected, various serious complications can arise." Fluid can accumulate in the lungs, or neurological damage can result if the blood vessels of the brain are affected. Acute kidney failure is also possible. About 20% of those affected die if the disease is left untreated. "If a diagnosis is made in time, there can be targeted treatment," Hörauf said. "If the disease is overlooked , however, it can very quickly take a severe turn." At first, symptoms are not specific, resembling those of the flu: sudden high fever, chills, headaches and muscle pain. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are also possible. Those who live near Frankfurt Airport have been advised to seek medical help if they have any suspicious symptoms Image: Rene Traut/Rene Traut Fotografie/picture alliance Frankfurt authorities tell public to seek advice in case of symptoms The Frankfurt Public Health Department has advised anybody who lives or works near Frankfurt Airport to seek medical attention immediately if they experience any such symptoms. Rapid diagnostic tests can provide evidence of malaria in human blood and then a blood test can help to confirm this. The RKI says treatment should take place at a hospital, which has expertise in tropical medicine. As summer comes to an end and temperatures cool in Germany , particularly at night, the conditions are becoming less favorable for mosquitoes and malaria parasites. However, experts warn that there could still be other cases of malaria in Germany despite the cooler weather. Plasmodium falciparum has an incubation period of seven to 15 days, so more than two weeks can pass between a mosquito transmitting malaria to somebody by biting them and the onset of symptoms. According to Hörauf, the biggest challenge is to ensure that people think malaria could be a possibility even if they have not traveled abroad. This article was translated from German. https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4608.text: Slovak MPs opened their first parliamentary session after the summer break on Tuesday, with almost 300 items on the agenda. These included a new Civil Code, restrictions on social media for children under 16, changes to voting from abroad and several constitutional amendments. On Wednesday, President Peter Pellegrini delivered his State of the Republic address. He described deep political polarisation as one of Slovakia’s most serious problems and criticised what he described as the opposition’s tendency to reject initiatives without discussion. Pellegrini also highlighted the Slovakia 2040 vision, prepared with experts from the Slovak Academy of Sciences. He called for broader political cooperation on long-term priorities, including innovation, energy, education and the transition towards a higher-value economy. Parliament also scheduled two extraordinary sessions on opposition motions to dismiss Economy Minister Denisa Saková and Interior Minister Matúš Šutaj Eštok. Source: TASR

Beállítom On the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian people’s uprising against Soviet oppression, commemorations were held throughout the country. One of the main events was a commemorative meeting of Parliament, followed by the Prime Minister's speech and concerts in Kossuth Square. In addition to Hungarian public officials, those present included András Baka, President of the Republic of Hungary; António Costa, President of the European Council; Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission; and Jens Stoltenberg, Norway’s Minister of Finance and the former Secretary General of NATO. Ágnes Forsthoffer, Speaker of the Parliament presided over the session which began with a viewing of original footage and photographs from October 23,1956, followed by a minute of silence in honor of the fallen heroes of the revolution. Hungarian President András Baka spoke first: “On October 23, 1956, the Hungarian people said ‘no’ to oppression, but the crowds that gathered in front of Parliament had no idea that oppression would follow just a few days later”. The head of state noted that even today, the tension on the faces of those who participated in the revolution can still be seen in the surviving photographs from that time. The President recounted the events from 70 years ago and stresed that during those difficult days, Hungarians relied on one another. András Baka noted that the presence of foreign guests at the commemoration made it a particularly meaningful occasion, as the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution holds universal significance and the uprising contributed to the creation of European unity. “Seventy years later, we Hungarians must also express our gratitude,” the head of state said before thanking the foreign nations which showed solidarity by taking in fleeing Hungarians in 1956. Turning to today, Baka said that political debates are a natural part of freedom. According to him, a nation cannot be the exclusive property of a single political community. The president noted that he is aware that fostering national unity is one of his responsibilities. According to him, 1956 was a moment of grace in Hungarian history. “If we have a society that supports us, then we will find a way towards each other,” he said, concluding his speech by noting that these memories need to be preserved so that future generations may draw inspiration from them. Overcoming fear is possible Ursula von der Leyen, the President of the European Commission, spoke next. She noted that overcoming fear is possible, and referred to the fact that the Hungarian people voted for change six months ago. She spoke of the new Hungarian government having strengthened anti-corruption regulations, Hungary having joined the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, and Hungarian students having returned to Europe through the Horizon and Erasmus programs in the past few months. “We missed them so much,” said the President of the European Commission, and concluded her speech with a quote from Albert Camus. Ursula von der Leyen alongside András Baka, Ágnes Forsthoffer, and Péter Magyar in Parliament – Photo: Bernadett Szabó / Reuters “Seventy years ago, the Hungarian people decided to launch an uprising against the communist dictatorship and the Soviet Union’s response was brutal,” the President of the European Council said in his speech. According to António Costa, the Hungarian people’s desire for freedom never faltered, and he noted that this was also the driving force behind the transition to democracy in 1989. Costa noted that Hungary’s accession to the European Union in 2004 also demonstrates that Europe’s strength lies in its diverse languages and cultures; in his view, this in no way threatens national identity, but rather allows European nations to strengthen one another. He noted that the Hungarian economy has nearly tripled in size since then and spoke about the close connection between prosperity and freedom. According to Costa, the European Union provides security, prosperity, and freedom for Hungarians as well. Magyar: The heroes of 1956 left behind a legacy for Hungarian leaders The official part of the program concluded with a speech from Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar on Kossuth Square. At the beginning of his speech, Péter Magyar greeted the strong and “now truly independent Hungary” and welcomed the foreign leaders attending the state ceremony. He also paid tribute to the surviving heroes of ’56 and thanked them for their courage. They showed what Hungarians are capable of when they stand up for one another. He described 1956 as perhaps one of the most important revolutions of the 20th century. Seventy years ago, university students, followed by factory workers and young men and women from Budapest marched side by side, though they did not yet know what the coming hours would bring. He believes that even if they had known what awaited them, they still wouldn’t have traded their fate for anything else. The crowd at Kossuth Square on 23 October 2026 – Photo: István Huszti / Telex Péter Magyar noted that in retrospect, every university remembers that it was their students' idea to join forces. He recalled the brutal massacre of protesters which happened during the revolution at the square and said that “There is nothing more moving and uplifting than being able to freely stand in this very same square exactly 70 years later". The Prime Minister spoke about the thirteen glorious days when Hungarians unanimously shouted, Russians, go home! “Those 13 days were a testimony to a clear conscience,” said Magyar. It took the army of a world empire—foreign weapons and tanks—to crush the revolution. He spoke of the days when the Soviet army crushed the fight for freedom. The overwhelming military force may have crushed the revolution, and they may have executed Imre Nagy and the other heroes, but they could never again take away from the Hungarian people the realization that we are capable of taking our destiny into our own hands. After the Hungarian Revolution, no decent person could ever again claim that communism would serve liberty and the people, because the workers themselves had risen up against the regime. According to Magyar, the heroes of 1956 also left behind a legacy for Hungarian leaders: namely, that their rule cannot be more important than their country’s freedom, no matter where they seek support. Let 1956 serve as a warning to them, for while power can be maintained for a time with foreign support, the freedom of the Hungarian people cannot be broken!-he said. “Those who make excuses for an aggressor have understood nothing of the message of 1956, whether they are Budapest or at a Parisian sidewalk café.” With this, the Prime Minister was referring to Viktor Orbán, who was photographed in Paris while the 1956 commemorations were going on in Hungary. “For many years, we were told the lie that the national holiday only belonged to one political side, but that’s over,” Magyar said, adding that Hungary is not a country of compromisers but wants to become a strong, independent, and intelligent nation. “Now it’s our turn to stand up for freedom,” Magyar continued. “We know what needs to be done: Hungary cannot be a country caught in the middle; it must not drift between East and West. We belong to a free, democratic Europe, and we want to be reliable allies who are sitting at the table with our heads held high. We want to become a wise, forward-looking nation.” He promised that they would never use the power they have been given against their own people, because governing is not about ruling, but about serving. He called on Hungarians to pull together. “We have so much to do together,” he said, adding that it would be good to leave our children a country we can be proud of. “This is our homeland, and we are willing to do anything for it,” Magyar said, concluding his speech with “Long live Hungarian freedom, gloria victis.” For more quick, accurate and impartial news from and about Hungary, subscribe to the Telex English newsletter! (Photo: Aeltegop, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons) FRANCE · ANALYSIS Key Facts What is happening The E5 defence ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom met in Paris on 26 October 2026 to coordinate support for Ukraine and European defence projects. Why it matters The format lets Europe’s five principal military powers align on capability gaps without waiting for wider NATO or EU consensus. The numbers Five countries issued one joint declaration on 26 October, calling Russia the “most acute and long-term threat” to Euro-Atlantic security. Who is who Catherine Vautrin, France’s armed forces minister, hosted the meeting. What to watch A date for the next E5 meeting, and whether the Ukraine air-defence plan gets national funding. What it means for you US defence contractors should read E5 announcements as political demand signals, not as funded NATO or EU procurement contracts. Latest: Le Pen Leads Every Runoff in New French Poll The E5 defence ministers are an informal coordination format bringing together France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. For US readers, the group matters because it is Europe’s most direct answer to Washington’s demand that allies carry more of their own defence burden. France has become a recurring venue for a compact European defence conversation that sits outside both NATO and the EU. This analysis explains what the E5 is, what it has decided and why its Paris meeting on 26 October 2026 signals where European defence demand may flow. The related Europe Intelligence Brief places the meeting in its wider context. What The E5 Actually Is The E5 is not a treaty-based alliance, an EU institution or a NATO command. France’s Defence Ministry calls it the European Group of Five, an informal ministerial format for rapid coordination among five of Europe’s principal military powers. Its members are France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. All five belong to NATO, while four are EU members and the United Kingdom sits outside the EU after Brexit. That composition gives the group a bridge-building role. It lets London participate in continental defence discussions while allowing Paris, Berlin, Rome and Warsaw to connect those talks to EU defence initiatives. The format has no standing secretariat, common budget or independent command structure. It operates through meetings convened by participating defence ministries, which makes it flexible but also harder to track than a formal institution. Poland’s Ministry of National Defence described the Kraków meeting of 20 February 2026 as the seventh E5 ministerial meeting since 2024. That frequency shows the format has become a recurring rhythm rather than a one-off summit. File photo: the Eiffel Tower in Paris. The E5 defence ministers met in the French capital on 26 October. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy . How The Format Developed The E5 emerged from three pressures. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine created an urgent need to coordinate military support among Europe’s largest defence powers. European governments also recognised gaps in air defence, ammunition, drones and other capabilities exposed by the war. Finally, Washington’s repeated demand that European allies assume a larger share of the defence burden pushed governments to find faster coordination mechanisms. The format should not be confused with other European groupings. The E5 comprises France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom, while the Weimar Triangle comprises only France, Germany and Poland. Those distinctions matter because they define who is in the room and what decisions can be made. The group’s previous Paris meeting was on 12 March 2025, according to France’s Defence Ministry. That meeting was hosted by Sébastien Lecornu, then France’s armed forces minister. What The E5 Has Decided The most concrete E5 output is the Low-Cost Effectors & Autonomous Platforms initiative, known as LEAP. Launched at the Kraków meeting on 20 February 2026, LEAP aims to develop lower-cost air-defence weapons and autonomous platforms capable of protecting NATO airspace. The British government announced LEAP as a multinational effort involving Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland. It links the programme directly to NATO air defence, but the initiative is not itself a NATO command or procurement agency. The logic behind LEAP is economic as much as military. Expensive missile interceptors can be consumed quickly against relatively inexpensive drones and cruise missiles, creating a cost imbalance that European governments want to correct. The Paris meeting of 26 October 2026 produced a joint declaration rather than a treaty. Reporting on it describes no new collective command and no binding troop commitment. What Paris Produced The joint declaration is dated 26 October 2026. It describes Russia as “the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability”. Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, said the group is working with Ukraine on an air-defence system to supplement existing defences, including US-made Patriot missiles (a long-range US air-defence system). Winter aid packages for Ukraine were also assembled. No new pledge amounts were reported. The Actors And What Each Wants Catherine Vautrin, France’s Minister for the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs, hosted the Paris meeting. France wants the E5 to anchor European defence cooperation while keeping Paris at the centre of the conversation. Germany brings industrial weight and budget capacity. Italy’s interest lies in Mediterranean security and ensuring that southern-flank concerns are not crowded out by the eastern focus on Ukraine. Poland is the group’s most exposed eastern member and the strongest advocate for urgent air-defence investment. The United Kingdom’s participation keeps Britain inside European defence planning despite Brexit, and it brings nuclear status and expeditionary experience. The Economic And Business Stakes For investors and defence contractors, the E5 is best read as a demand signal rather than a procurement pipeline. An E5 announcement may signal political support for a capability area, but it does not automatically constitute a funded programme or guaranteed order. The capability areas most likely to benefit are those where European governments want faster and larger-scale production. Air defence, drones, autonomous systems, ammunition, sensors and related electronics sit at the top of that list. Pooling demand among five large defence markets may help companies reach production volumes that individual national orders cannot provide. That is the industrial logic behind LEAP and similar cooperative projects. The distinction between E5, NATO and EU matters commercially. A project launched through the E5 does not automatically qualify for EU financing through the European Defence Fund or become a NATO procurement programme. US contractors should therefore treat E5 statements as early indicators of European intent. The gap between political announcement and funded contract can be wide, and the E5 has no common budget to close it. What It Means For The United States And Latin America Washington has long pushed Europe to carry more of its own defence burden. The E5 is the clearest European institutional response to that pressure, even though it remains informal and politically driven. The group does not compete with NATO’s collective-defence system. NATO remains responsible for Article 5 (its mutual-defence clause), integrated military command, common defence planning and alliance-wide operational requirements. The E5 operates below that level. It helps participating governments coordinate positions, launch joint capability projects and shape proposals that may later support NATO requirements. For Latin American readers, the E5 matters as a case study in how middle powers organise defence cooperation without waiting for a superpower. Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Colombia face their own capability gaps, though their security environment differs sharply from Europe’s. The E5 also shows how informal formats can move faster than treaty-based institutions. That lesson may resonate in regions where formal security organisations are slow or politically constrained. The Scenarios The stabilising scenario is that the E5 becomes a reliable pre-negotiation chamber. Five large European governments would align on Ukraine, air defence and industrial scale before taking positions into wider NATO or EU discussions. That would make European defence cooperation faster without creating a new bureaucracy. It would also give Washington a clearer European counterpart on burden-sharing questions. The tipping scenario is that the E5 remains a talking shop. Without a common budget, secretariat or binding procurement mechanism, its announcements could fail to translate into funded programmes. A second risk is duplication. If E5 projects compete with EU or NATO initiatives rather than feeding them, the result could be fragmentation rather than scale. The most likely path lies between those poles. The E5 will probably continue as a recurring political forum that occasionally produces concrete initiatives such as LEAP, while the harder work of funding and procurement stays with national governments and existing institutions. What It Means for You If you invest in or sell to the defence sector, track E5 statements as early indicators of European demand. The capability areas named in E5 announcements are where European governments want faster production, even if contracts lag behind. If you follow US foreign policy, the E5 is evidence that Europe is building a more credible defence pillar within NATO. That may reduce pressure on Washington to lead every European security response. If you do business in Europe, the E5’s informality is a feature, not a bug. It allows quick political alignment without the legal constraints of EU or NATO processes, but it also means decisions are not automatically enforceable. What Is Not Known Official sources say little about how the E5 began, so its origins are less documented than its recent activity. The group has no common budget, so its financial footprint cannot be quantified as of October 2026. The available statements do not establish that the E5 has created a new collective military command or made a legally binding commitment to deploy troops. Those claims should be treated as unconfirmed unless a separate official communiqué emerges. We have not found an announced date or venue for the next E5 meeting as of 26 October 2026. Watch for changes in ministerial participation. Further turnover could shift the group’s priorities. Frequently Asked Questions What is the E5 group of defence ministers? The E5 is an informal ministerial format bringing together the defence ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. It coordinates on Ukraine, European defence capabilities and defence-industrial cooperation. Is the E5 part of NATO or the EU? No. The E5 is separate from both NATO and the EU. All five members belong to NATO, and four are EU members, but the format itself has no treaty basis, standing secretariat or common budget. What has the E5 decided so far?
